sources.title: From damage to discovery via virtual unwrapping: Reading the scroll from En-Gedi
sources.locator: Introduction; Virtual unwrapping; The volumetric scan; Segmentation; Texturing; Flattening; Results; Discussion
sources.summary: The charred parchment fragmented on touch. Micro-CT supplied a volume; segmentation located surfaces, texturing sampled intensities, and flattening formed readable images. Ink was denser in the scan; metal content was inferred, not chemically established. Recovered Hebrew columns were identified as Leviticus. The object was not physically unrolled. Transformation provenance enables checking extracted text against scan voxels. Transport and handling still carry risk. Dating methods differ; no exact age used.

sources.title: Living Virtually: Creating and Intervacing Digital Surrogates of Textual Data Embedded (Hidden) in Cultural Heritage Artifacts
sources.locator: Project description: Intact Scrolls; True Born-Digital Text; ink detectability discussion
sources.summary: Investigators describe noninvasive volumetric imaging and digital surfaces flattened into images. En-Gedi yielded identifiable Leviticus text. They stress that ink is not guaranteed to appear in a volume, contrasting the different carbon-ink problem at Herculaneum. This is an investigator account of methods, not independent replication or current completeness of Herculaneum recovery.

definitions: The burned En-Gedi scroll was too fragile to physically open safely.
Fragile conservation object; noninvasive scanning still required careful handling.
The charred En-Gedi fragments continued to disintegrate when touched.
Reported condition of this particular material, not all burned manuscripts.
Researchers used X-ray micro-CT to acquire a three-dimensional volume of the En-Gedi scroll.
A scan is not an instant readable photograph of a closed page.
Researchers traced and modeled surviving parchment surfaces within the scan.
Complex piecewise segmentation, not automatic perfect detection of every sheet.
The En-Gedi ink responded more densely than surrounding materials in the micro-CT scan.
Composition was not chemically established; do not assert iron or lead as a measured fact.
The pipeline assigned scan intensities to modeled surfaces and flattened them into readable images.
Algorithmic approximations and merge steps omitted from animation but not denied.
The recovered Hebrew text was identified as part of the Book of Leviticus.
No superlative, age claim, religious proof or complete original manuscript claim.
The En-Gedi text was recovered without physically unrolling the scroll.
Does not mean never transported or touched.
Virtual unwrapping requires a scan that makes the writing detectable.
Not a universal scanner for every ink and material.
The ink was proven to contain iron.
Excluded: paper infers possible metal, chemistry remains unknown.
lines: This burned scroll was too fragile to open. Scientists read it anyway.
The En-Gedi scroll crumbled when it was touched.
Researchers scanned it with X-rays, building a three-dimensional map.
Inside that scan, they traced the surviving layers.
In this scroll, the ink showed up more densely than the parchment.
They mapped that signal onto digital surfaces, then flattened them into readable images.
The recovered Hebrew text came from the Book of Leviticus.
This worked because the ink was detectable in the scan. Different materials need different approaches.
They revealed surviving writing without unrolling the fragile original.
objectives: Establish impossible-seeming task with immediate truthful resolution promise.
Explain why physical opening is unavailable.
Change the object of work from artifact to volume.
Trace the hidden page, not a generic see-through photograph.
Show ink contrast without asserting chemical composition.
Carry the same sample marks through surface extraction and flattening.
Identify result without theology, invented transcription or superlatives.
Return to unchanged closed artifact and digital image together.
